Hi all! I am considering using Lean to teach an undergraduate course. In this setting, I would use Lean _not_ as a proof assistant, but instead "merely" as a pure functional programming language. (The reason to use Lean is to still benefit from its great IDE integration, and give a smooth path towards formal proofs later on.) I don't even need IO, as we will be running everything using #eval. Indeed, I want to only use the subset of Lean's type theory that can be encoded by ordinary FP languages, such as OCaml, and not focus on soundness -- even redefining def to partial def so that students may write and evaluate code without worrying about termination, and carefully walling off the available libraries so that students don't run into dependent types.

Are there prior resources for / experiences of this mode of using Lean? I can see multiple solutions here -- two that spring to mind are a completely fresh user syntax that elaborates to Lean functions, or a collection of macros that provides a "walled garden" for Lean
@Sebastian Erdweg might be available to comment on using Lean as an undergrad FP in general though I don't think he restricted the language for his course

Yup, if there is wisdom that a technological solution is unnecessary, that would be helpful too. The failure mode I am trying to alleviate is a student accidentally running into dependent type messiness without a clear error message that tells them they are doing something wrong

Hi Joshua! I taught an undergrad course about functional programming last semester at KIT. We used Lean 4 without any restrictions (including parts of the standard library), but I only taught and showed students non-dependent FP concepts and types. Some observations:

I don't think we experienced many issues of using unrestricted Lean. In particular, students did not accidentally ran into dependent types. Of course, some type errors are more cryptic than would be necessary if we had used a teaching subset of Lean, but the students managed as far as I know. Possibly AI helped making sense of complex type errors.

I think there are also some important opportunities when using unrestricted Lean:

  • In the second week, we explored structural and generative recursion. We discussed why termination checking succeeded in the non-recursive examples (data grunshing with list processing pipelines) from week 1, and the structurally recursive examples from week 2. The way I framed it is that termination checking is an extra goodie that students can opt out off using partial def. (I think students were impressed that so many of our functions actually had guaranteed termination, contrasting their intuition from the halting problem)
  • Inspired students can easily venture off to explore more of the language. In week 5, we discussed complexity and performance, and we benchmarked our own List.length and List.reverse against the standard library. While we did not do any theorem proving, this was a good opportunity to show students some of the theorems in the library, in particular that length = lengthTR, justifying that the compiler replaces one by the other. Some students went down that rabbit hole on their own, which was nice.
  • Availability of libraries: Using unrestricted Lean makes it easy to use libraries. For example, we used plausible for property-based testing.
  • I wanted to show advanced non-dependent FP concepts, such as abstract types, type classes, monads, and task parallelization. Adding all of them to your own teaching language becomes a nuisance.

Happy to have a chat @Joshua Gancher if you're interested
Hi Sebastian - thanks for the insights. I am pleased to hear that students didn’t run into isssues using Lean from the get go!
